claims.text: The elevated-temperature wear transition in FeNiCrCoCu coatings is driven by a thermally activated reduction in stacking-fault energy.
Reduced stacking-fault energy suppresses deformation twinning in FeNiCrCoCu.
The temperature-induced stacking-fault-energy change promotes rapid dislocation climb and cross-slip.
Dislocation climb and cross-slip accelerate lattice disorder and softening.
The FeNiCrCoCu coating is FCC at room temperature.
At 300 K, the coating has a high dislocation density and stable stacking-fault structures.
Sliding friction can generate substantial contact heating that softens a high-entropy alloy and increases its wear rate.
The onset of significant lattice softening in the target coating is expected between 400 and 600 K.
Low-temperature FeNiCrCoCu has relatively high stacking-fault energy compared with Al-containing variants.
Deformation twinning and retained high dislocation density enhance work hardening and wear resistance at low temperature.
Increasing temperature causes dynamic recovery and dislocation annihilation, preventing the coating from sustaining a high dislocation density.
Thermal softening causes a sharp decline in hardness and elastic modulus and facilitates adhesive wear and material loss.
A critical temperature exists at which the FeNiCrCoCu wear rate increases by an order of magnitude.
Below the critical temperature, wear is dominated by mild abrasion with stable subsurface hardening.
Above the critical temperature, wear changes to severe adhesive or oxidative wear.
At 300 K, FeNiCrCoCu has stable wear resistance and a high elastic modulus.
Room-temperature stability in FeNiCrCoCu is attributable to lattice distortion and high defect-migration barriers analogous to those reported for NiCoFeCrPd.
Formation of a BCC phase in AlxCoCrFeNi can increase hardness and reduce wear rate.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to FCC-dominant coatings in which twinning is a primary low-temperature hardening mechanism.
